questions.question: Which part of an airliner keeps the nose from swinging left and right on its own, and carries the rudder?
options: The vertical stabilizer
The rudder itself
The horizontal stabilizer
The winglets
questions.explanation: The vertical stabilizer is the fixed fin. It gives stability in yaw, and the rudder is hinged to its trailing edge. The rudder itself is the moving surface, not the fixed one. The horizontal stabilizer works in pitch, and the winglets weaken the wingtip vortices.

questions.question: The pilot pulls the control column back. What do the elevator and the aircraft do?
options: The elevator trailing edge goes up, the tail is pushed down, and the nose pitches up
The elevator trailing edge goes down, the tail is pushed up, and the nose pitches up
The elevator trailing edge goes up, the tail is pushed up, and the nose pitches down
The two elevators move in opposite directions, and the aircraft rolls
questions.explanation: When the trailing edge of the elevator goes up, the tail makes a downward force. The tail moves down, and the nose pitches up about the center of gravity. A tail pushed up would lower the nose. The surfaces that move in opposite directions to roll the aircraft are the ailerons.

questions.question: A top view of an airplane is drawn as seen from above, with the nose toward the left of the page. Where is the right wing, and toward which edge of the page does a positive yaw turn the nose?
options: Wing at the top; nose toward the top
Wing at the bottom; nose toward the bottom
Wing at the top; nose toward the bottom
Wing at the bottom; nose toward the top
questions.explanation: Face the nose, which points left, and your right hand is toward the top of the page. Positive yaw swings the nose toward the right wing, so the nose moves up the page. A right wing at the bottom describes a view from below, and a nose turning away from the right wing reverses the sense of positive yaw.

questions.question: Why can a tail-dragger fall into a ground loop more easily than a tricycle-gear aircraft?
options: Its center of gravity is behind the main wheels, so a swerve, once started, grows
Its center of gravity is ahead of the main wheels, so its weight pushes it further around
Its tail wheel cannot be steered, so the pilot has no control on the ground
It sits nose up, so its wing makes lift on the ground and lifts the main wheels
questions.explanation: On a tail-dragger the main wheels are ahead of the center of gravity, and once a swerve starts, the weight keeps pushing the aircraft further around. On a tricycle the center of gravity is ahead of the main wheels, and the weight keeps the aircraft straight. Many tail wheels can be steered, and the nose-up stance is not the cause.

questions.question: A wing has a span of 72 ft and an area of 480 ft². What is its aspect ratio?
questions.explanation: AR = b²/S = 72 × 72/480 = 5,184/480 = 10.8. If you use half the span, you get 36 × 36/480 = 2.70. 480/72 = 6.67 ft is the average chord, not a ratio, and 5.40 comes from dividing by twice the area.

questions.section: Airfoil geometry and NACA four-digit airfoils
questions.question: An airfoil is a NACA 2318 with a chord of 2.0 m. How large is its maximum camber, and where is it?
options: 0.04 m, at 0.6 m from the leading edge
0.04 m, at 0.06 m from the leading edge
0.06 m, at 0.04 m from the leading edge
0.36 m, at 0.6 m from the leading edge
questions.explanation: M = 2, so the camber is 2% of 2.0 m, or 0.04 m. P = 3, so it sits 3 tenths, 30%, of the chord from the leading edge, 0.6 m. If you read P as 3%, you get 0.06 m. If you read the second digit as the camber and the first as its position, both in percent, you get 0.06 m at 0.04 m. And 0.36 m is the thickness, 18% of the chord.

questions.question: On the Ariane 5 core stage, which tank is the larger one, and why?
options: The liquid-hydrogen tank, because hydrogen needs far more volume for its mass
The liquid-oxygen tank, because the stage carries more oxygen than hydrogen by mass
The liquid-oxygen tank, because the oxidizer must last longer than the fuel
Both tanks are the same size, because the engine burns equal volumes of each
questions.explanation: In the first version of the stage the hydrogen tank held 390 m³ and the oxygen tank 120 m³, although the oxygen had 5.1 times the mass. Oxygen is dense, and a large mass of it fits in a small volume. A larger mass does not mean a larger tank. The engine burns both propellants for the whole burn, in neither equal volumes nor equal masses.

questions.question: A mission profile has five segments: takeoff, climb, cruise, descent, and landing. How are its points numbered, and what is W2?
options: From 0 to 5; W2 is the weight at the end of the climb
From 1 to 5; W2 is the weight at the end of the climb
From 0 to 5; W2 is the weight at the start of the climb
From 0 to 4; W2 is the weight during the cruise
questions.explanation: We number the ends of the segments, starting from 0 at the start of the takeoff. Five segments give six points, 0 to 5, and point 2 is the end of the second segment, the climb. If you number the segments instead of their ends, you get 1 to 5 or 0 to 4. The start of the climb is point 1.
